subChunks.title: ArrayList

storyBeats.text: Eldrin reaches into his robe and pulls out what appears to be a small leather pouch — then keeps pulling, drawing out scroll after scroll far beyond what should fit.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: An ArrayList is an enchanted bag. You can keep adding scrolls without ever running out of space — it expands as needed. Unlike the fixed shelf, this container is dynamic.

storyBeats.label: The enchanted bag

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Notice the angle brackets — ArrayList<String>. That is the type parameter. It locks the bag to hold only Strings. Try adding a number, and the compiler refuses.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Create an ArrayList<String> containing four wizard names: "Merlin", "Gandalf", "Dumbledore", "Saruman". Remove "Saruman", then print each remaining name on its own line.
guidedPractice.hint: Use contains() or remove by index. Remember remove(int) removes by index while remove(Object) removes by value.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain ArrayList in Java. How does it differ from a plain array, and what are the three most commonly used methods?

questions.prompt: Which method returns the number of elements in an ArrayList?
questions.explanation: For ArrayList (and all Java collections) use size(). Arrays use .length (a field, not a method).
remove(1) removes the element at index 1 (value 20), leaving [10, 30].

questions.prompt: ArrayList<int> is a valid declaration in Java.
questions.explanation: Generics require reference types, not primitives. Use ArrayList<Integer> (the wrapper class). Java auto-boxes int ↔ Integer automatically.

subChunks.title: HashMap

storyBeats.text: Eldrin gestures to a magical registry on the wall — a vast tome where every wizard's name is instantly linked to their power level.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: A HashMap is the Academy registry. You look up any entry by name — the key — and instantly receive the value it maps to. No searching, no counting positions. Direct access.

storyBeats.label: The registry

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Always check for null or use getOrDefault when looking up keys that may not exist. A null result where you expected a number will give you a NullPointerException — the most common mistake with maps.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Create a HashMap<String, Integer> mapping three spell names to their power levels: "Fireball" → 75, "Ice Lance" → 60, "Thunder" → 90. Print the power of "Ice Lance", then print whether "Shadow Bolt" is in the map.
guidedPractice.hint: Use containsKey("Shadow Bolt") to check for membership.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain HashMap — what is a key, what is a value, and how does retrieval work? Why is HashMap faster than searching a list?

questions.prompt: What does map.get("missingKey") return if the key doesn't exist?
questions.explanation: HashMap.get() returns null for missing keys. Use getOrDefault(key, fallback) to avoid dealing with null.
Putting the same key twice overwrites the value. So "a" maps to 99. The map has 2 unique keys, so size is 2.

questions.prompt: A HashMap guarantees that entries are iterated in the order they were inserted.
questions.explanation: HashMap does not guarantee insertion order. Use LinkedHashMap for insertion-ordered iteration.

subChunks.title: Iterating Collections & Choosing the Right One

storyBeats.text: Eldrin spreads four containers on the workbench: a fixed stone shelf, an enchanted bag, a magical registry, and a glowing orb that only holds unique crystals.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The wisest choice of container is made before you start filling it. Ask yourself: do I need order? Do I need fast lookups by name? Do I need unique elements only? Each answer points to a different container.

storyBeats.label: Iterating both

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Using a HashMap where an ArrayList would do is like carrying a full registry to check three names. Know your tools and use the right one.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Create an ArrayList<Integer> of five numbers: 3, 1, 4, 1, 5. Then create a HashMap<String, Integer> with two entries: "min" → 1, "max" → 5. Print the list size, then print the map's max entry.
guidedPractice.hint: Use list.size() and map.get("max") for the two print statements.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Describe three different Java collection types and explain a real-world scenario where you would choose each one.

questions.prompt: You need to track whether each student has submitted their assignment. Which collection is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: A HashMap<String, Boolean> lets you look up any student's status by name in O(1). An ArrayList would require O(n) searching.

options: Replace 'm' with 'm.keySet()' in the for-each (or use m.entrySet())
questions.answer: Replace 'm' with 'm.keySet()' in the for-each (or use m.entrySet())
questions.explanation: You cannot iterate a HashMap directly. You must iterate m.keySet(), m.values(), or m.entrySet().

questions.prompt: Your application stores a leaderboard with thousands of player scores. You need to: (1) quickly find any player's score by username, and (2) display the top 10 players sorted by score. Which approach best handles both needs?
options: Store scores in a HashMap<String,Integer> for fast lookups; separately maintain a sorted List for the leaderboard display
Store scores in a sorted ArrayList only
Use an array of player objects sorted by score
Use two ArrayLists — one for names, one for scores
questions.answer: Store scores in a HashMap<String,Integer> for fast lookups; separately maintain a sorted List for the leaderboard display
questions.explanation: A HashMap handles O(1) lookup by username. For sorted display, maintain a sorted list or sort on demand. Using a single sorted list for both would give O(n) lookups.
